condition.mesh_scope_note: A common genetically determined, chronic, inflammatory skin disease characterized by rounded erythematous, dry, scaling patches. The lesions have a predilection for nails, scalp, genitalia, extensor surfaces, and the lumbosacral region. Accelerated epidermopoiesis is considered to be the fundamental pathologic feature in psoriasis.

executive_summary.headline: Plaque psoriasis is a crowded, efficacy-saturated market where the next competitive battle is oral convenience: icotrokinra's head-to-head against deucravacitinib and a wave of Chinese TYK2 followers will reshape the oral segment, while durability, obesity and special populations remain under-served.

key_takeaways.text: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated systemic inflammatory disease. US adult prevalence is 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%), about 7.55 million adults (NHANES 2011-2014), and Western Europe prevalence is 1.92%.
Biologics have set a high efficacy bar. In a 2020 network meta-analysis, PASI 90 at weeks 10-16 was 71.6% for risankizumab, 70.8% for brodalumab, 70.6% for ixekizumab and 67.3% for guselkumab.

Guidelines are shifting toward earlier advanced therapy. AAD-NPF supports biologics as a first-line option, and the German S3 guideline highlights first-line biologics or novel small molecules, adds bimekizumab and deucravacitinib, and sets PASI 90 or absolute PASI <2 as desirable goals.
The pipeline of 63 active trials is dominated by oral TYK2 inhibitors, most in Ph3, while deucravacitinib is already standard of care. This creates a crowded follower class.

Head-to-head trials against standard-of-care agents are the key differentiation evidence. Examples include icotrokinra vs deucravacitinib, picankibart vs secukinumab/ixekizumab, netakimab vs adalimumab, and bimekizumab and deucravacitinib vs ustekinumab.

Most discontinuations reflect enrollment difficulty or business decisions rather than target invalidation. Low enrollment ended placebo-controlled secukinumab and brodalumab Ph3 trials in the crowded field.

white_space.text: Durable remission is unmet. On-treatment remission (BSA 0% or IGA 0 for at least 6 months) was only recently standardized, and precision medicine for durability remains a research goal.
Obesity reduces biologic efficacy and drug survival, leaving room for therapies with weight-independent efficacy.
Pediatric psoriasis has few data on epidemiology, comorbidity and therapy, and lacks international management guidelines. This supports dedicated pediatric programs.

Special populations such as HIV-associated psoriasis show higher failure rates and need monitoring for opportunistic infections. Patients with multiple comorbidities need safer targeted agents and care models that address systemic inflammation.

Heterogeneous severity classifications can miscategorize patients and lead to undertreatment. The IPC dichotomous topical-vs-systemic framework opens earlier systemic use for patients with BSA >10%, special-area involvement or topical failure.

competitive_threats.text: Janssen's oral IL-23 receptor peptide icotrokinra seeks biologic-like IL-23 blockade in a pill and is being tested head-to-head against deucravacitinib. Janssen is the most active sponsor, with 5 active Ph2/3 trials.
Multiple TYK2 followers are running Ph3 trials directly against deucravacitinib, including TQH3906 and D-2570, alongside Takeda's zasocitinib and Alumis' envudeucitinib.
Biosimilars and follow-ons will pressure pricing in the IL-17A and IL-23 classes: CT-P55 is being tested against Cosentyx and QL2106 against Tremfya.
Chinese companies make up a large share of leading sponsors (Hengrui, Haisco, Hansoh, InventisBio, InnoCare, CSPC Ouyi, Innovent and others), many with undisclosed-mechanism assets.
Picankibart is challenging IL-17A inhibitors head-to-head against secukinumab and ixekizumab. Bimekizumab's dual IL-17A/F blockade is being tested against ustekinumab.

overview.text: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease and the most common psoriasis variant, with substantial physical, psychological and social impact.
Psoriasis is regarded as a systemic inflammatory disease with a major genetic component, associated with psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic, hepatic and psychological comorbidity.
Management is tailored to severity: topicals for mild disease; oral systemics and biologics (TNF, IL-17, IL-23, IL-12/23) for moderate-to-severe disease.

severity_stratification.definition: International Psoriasis Council Delphi consensus: systemic candidates meet at least one of BSA >10%, involvement of special areas, or failure of topical therapy; replaces mild/moderate/severe categories.
Conventionally managed with topical therapy as first-line (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, calcineurin inhibitors).
Conventionally requires systemic therapy (oral agents or biologics); biologics are an option for first-line treatment per AAD-NPF guidelines.

addressable_population.text: Basis: about 3.0% US adult prevalence (about 7.55 million adults); the share eligible for systemic therapy is not quantified in the sources.
Systemic-therapy candidates are defined by BSA >10%, special-area involvement or topical failure, rather than by a fixed severity share.
Adult-focused guidelines address moderate-to-severe disease; psoriasis occurs more often in adults than in children (up to 2% of European children).

pathophysiology.text: Strong genetic predisposition: HLA-C*06:02 shows the strongest association, particularly in early-onset disease; loci include IL23A, IL12B and IL17RA, linking to IL-23/Th17 dysregulation.

Dendritic cells, Th17 cells and keratinocytes form a pathogenic triad: dendritic cell TNF-α and IL-23 drive Th17 cells producing IL-17, IFN-γ and IL-22, causing keratinocyte activation and hyperproliferation.
Keratinocytes initiate and maintain inflammation, releasing antimicrobial peptides and danger signals that amplify the immune loop.
ILC3 cells producing IL-17 and IL-22 can induce psoriatic rash without T-cell/antigen interaction and are increased in blood and skin.
Environmental triggers contribute, including stress, which 31-88% of patients report as a trigger, and microbiota changes.

clinical_manifestations.text: Presents with rounded erythematous, dry, scaling plaques, with predilection for nails, scalp, genitalia, extensor surfaces and lumbosacral region.
Psoriasis is clinically heterogeneous: plaque, flexural, guttate, pustular or erythrodermic forms; plaque psoriasis is the most common.
Generalized pustular psoriasis is a distinct, rare, potentially life-threatening entity with sterile pustules, differing from plaque psoriasis.
Childhood disease resembles adult disease but with smaller plaques, finer scales and more facial and guttate involvement.

comorbidities.text: Psoriatic arthritis affects about 19.7% of psoriasis patients (pooled; 3.3% in under-18s).
Cardiometabolic disease, including cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome, is associated with psoriasis, particularly severe disease.
Psychiatric disorders and depression are associated with psoriasis.
Obesity is strongly associated with psoriasis and reduces biologic efficacy and drug survival.
Other associations include gastrointestinal disease, kidney disease, malignancy and infection.

prognosis.text: Psoriasis is a lifelong, chronic, relapsing-remitting disease.
Comorbidities contribute to increased morbidity and mortality; patients have higher cerebrovascular and cardiovascular disease and a younger age at death.
On-treatment remission is defined as BSA 0% or IGA 0 maintained for at least 6 months; PASI 75 is the minimum therapeutic target and PASI 90 or PASI <2 desirable.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: Remission benchmarks (BSA 0% or IGA 0 for 6 months) were only recently standardized; precision medicine to enhance treatment durability is an ongoing research goal.
unmet_needs.clinical_impact: Lack of benchmarks hinders aligned expectations and long-term coverage decisions.
unmet_needs.opportunity: Agents achieving durable complete clearance and sustained remission.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: Obesity decreases efficacy of biologics and may decrease efficacy and potentiate side effects of conventional therapies; it also reduces drug survival.
unmet_needs.clinical_impact: Reduced response in a large comorbid subgroup.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: Special populations such as HIV-associated psoriasis show higher failure rates and need monitoring for opportunistic infections; paradoxical psoriasis occurs with some drugs.
unmet_needs.clinical_impact: Limited options and careful monitoring in complex patients.
unmet_needs.opportunity: Safer targeted agents for patients with comorbidities.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: No clear guidelines on vascular testing in psoriasis, and treatment must be tailored around multiple comorbidities.
unmet_needs.clinical_impact: Increased cardiovascular and psychiatric burden persists.
unmet_needs.opportunity: Therapies and care models addressing systemic inflammation and comorbidities.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: Heterogeneous severity classifications ignore special areas and treatment history, so patients may be miscategorized.
unmet_needs.opportunity: Earlier systemic or biologic use and new agents (e.g. Tyk2, IL-23R inhibitors) for patients meeting systemic criteria.

unmet_needs.current_limitation: Few data on epidemiology, comorbidity and therapy in children; international management guidelines are lacking.
unmet_needs.clinical_impact: Treatment choices rely on limited evidence.

algorithm_summary.text: The International Psoriasis Council Delphi consensus proposes a dichotomous classification in place of mild/moderate/severe: patients are candidates for topical therapy or for systemic therapy. Systemic candidates meet at least one criterion: BSA >10%, involvement of special areas, or failure of topical therapy.

Topical agents (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, calcineurin inhibitors, keratolytics) remain the mainstay for mild psoriasis. AAD-NPF guidelines recommend biologics as an option for first-line treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.

The updated German S3 guideline (adapted from EuroGuiDerm) more prominently highlights first-line use of biologics or novel targeted small molecules and has added bimekizumab and deucravacitinib. It defines PASI 75 as the minimum therapeutic target, with PASI 90 or absolute PASI <2 as desirable goals.

The 2025 French guidelines recommend methotrexate, adalimumab or ustekinumab as primary systemic treatment for patients without symptomatic comorbidities. The NPF consensus defines on-treatment remission as BSA 0% or IGA 0 maintained for at least 6 months on treatment.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Mild disease / candidates for topical therapy (BSA <=10%, no special-area involvement, no topical failure)
lines_of_therapy.rationale: Topical therapy is the mainstay for mild psoriasis; the IPC dichotomy assigns patients not meeting systemic criteria to topical therapy.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults (systemic candidates: BSA >10%, special areas, or topical failure)
lines_of_therapy.rationale: AAD-NPF guidelines recommend biologics as first-line options for moderate-to-severe disease. The German S3 guideline highlights first-line biologics or novel small molecules.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Adults with moderate-to-severe psoriasis without symptomatic comorbidities (French guidelines 2025)
lines_of_therapy.rationale: The French working group recommends these as the primary systemic treatment.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Inadequate response, low disease activity, or need to switch, long-term management of moderate-to-severe disease
therapies: Switch to another biologic or targeted agent
lines_of_therapy.rationale: EuroGuiDerm covers conventional and biologic systemics. French guidelines include recommendations for insufficient response. Biologics show a longer time to relapse than oral systemic agents after discontinuation.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Guttate psoriasis not controlled with topicals/phototherapy
lines_of_therapy.rationale: A systematic review proposes methotrexate or cyclosporine as second-line for guttate psoriasis. First-line is topical corticosteroids and calcipotriol with phototherapy.
The proposed algorithm positions biologics as third-line for severe and refractory guttate psoriasis.

lines_of_therapy.setting: Patients with obesity (reduced efficacy of biologics) and special populations such as ICI-induced psoriasis
therapies: Weight control with optimized systemic therapy
Non-steroid systemic agents for ICI-induced psoriasis
lines_of_therapy.rationale: Obesity decreases biologic efficacy and weight control is vital. For ICI-induced psoriasis, systemic agents may be used without appreciable loss of ICI effectiveness, with non-steroid agents preferred over systemic corticosteroids.

moa.mechanism: Neutralize TNF-alpha, a cytokine produced by dendritic cells that promotes T cell differentiation toward TH17 cells.
moa.downstream_effects: Reduces upstream drivers of the IL-23/IL-17 axis, decreasing keratinocyte activation and skin inflammation.

moa.mechanism: Binds the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23.
moa.downstream_effects: Dampens IL-23-driven TH17 differentiation and IL-17/IL-22 production.

moa.mechanism: Selectively inhibit the p19 subunit of IL-23, produced by dendritic cells.
moa.downstream_effects: Reduces TH17 and ILC3 maturation and IL-17/IL-22 output, resolving keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Longest time to relapse after discontinuation among biologics.

moa.mechanism: Inhibit IL-17 cytokines (brodalumab acts at the IL-17 pathway).
moa.downstream_effects: Blocks the effector cytokine from TH17 cells and ILC3s on keratinocytes, reducing epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation.
Modulates intracellular inflammatory signalling (PDE-4 pathway) in psoriasis pathogenesis.

moa.mechanism: Tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor, acting in the JAK-STAT signalling pathway.
moa.downstream_effects: Dampens cytokine signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway implicated in psoriasis.

pipeline_summary.text: The pipeline is dominated by oral TYK2 inhibitors (zasocitinib, envudeucitinib, ICP-488, SYHX1901, TQH3906, D-2570 and others), most in Ph3. This is crowded, and deucravacitinib is already SoC.

Head-to-head designs against SoC are the strongest evidence. They include icotrokinra versus deucravacitinib, picankibart versus secukinumab and ixekizumab, netakimab versus adalimumab, and deucravacitinib and bimekizumab versus ustekinumab.
The oral IL-23 receptor peptide icotrokinra aims to pair biologic-like IL-23 pathway blockade with oral convenience.
Several assets are biosimilars or follow-ons (CT-P55 versus Cosentyx, QL2106 versus Tremfya) that differentiate on cost and access rather than efficacy.
Many early assets (e.g., CMS-D001, WD-890, HS-20118) are placebo-controlled with undisclosed mechanisms. Their differentiation versus SoC cannot yet be assessed.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 program with placebo-controlled and dose-comparison designs, plus a placebo- and active-controlled study against deucravacitinib (SoC). Head-to-head versus an oral SoC is stronger evidence than placebo alone.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Aims to bring IL-23 pathway blockade, the mechanism of IL-23 p19 biologics, in an oral form, and to beat the oral TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib head-to-head.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trials are placebo-controlled or dose-comparison, plus one single-arm study. No head-to-head SoC comparator is listed in these trials, so the evidence is weaker.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Competes with deucravacitinib in the oral TYK2 class. The sources do not support a claim of superiority. Positioned as an oral alternative to injectable biologics.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trials with placebo and an active ustekinumab (SoC) comparator. These are new studies of an already-approved SoC agent.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Already part of SoC as an oral targeted agent. The head-to-head design against the IL-12/23 biologic ustekinumab tests oral efficacy versus a biologic.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: One Ph3 trial is head-to-head against active IL-17 biologics (secukinumab, ixekizumab; SoC), which is strong evidence. A second Ph3 trial is placebo-controlled.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Aims to show that IL-23 p19 inhibition is superior to or at least competitive with IL-17A inhibitors. The sources do not state dosing-interval claims.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Trial designs include an active ustekinumab (SoC) comparator, an active clobetasol comparator, no-treatment and single-arm designs. Evidence quality varies across studies.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Dual IL-17A/IL-17F inhibition is a more complete blockade of the IL-17 pathway than IL-17A-only agents. The trials explore use in additional settings beyond standard use.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trial with placebo and an active adalimumab (SoC) comparator, so head-to-head evidence against a TNF inhibitor is planned.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Follows the IL-17A class, which is already established as SoC. It aims to beat the TNF-alpha inhibitor adalimumab.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trial with active deucravacitinib 6 mg (SoC) and placebo arms. This is a head-to-head against the approved TYK2 inhibitor.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Aims to match or beat deucravacitinib within the oral TYK2 class. The sources do not give differentiating data.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 and Ph2 trials with placebo and an active BMS-986165 (deucravacitinib code name; SoC) arm.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: A TYK2 follower that tests itself against deucravacitinib. It aims for comparable or better efficacy in an oral form.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trial against EU-approved Cosentyx, a biosimilar equivalence design.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Aims for equivalence to secukinumab rather than superiority. Differentiation is mainly access and cost.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trial against active Tremfya (guselkumab), most likely an equivalence design.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Likely a guselkumab biosimilar or follow-on. Differentiation is cost and access rather than a new mechanism.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 trial with placebo only, with no active SoC comparator. Evidence is weaker than head-to-head.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: An oral TYK2 option intended to compete with deucravacitinib. The sources do not support a claim of superiority.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 single-arm trial, which is the weakest design.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: Follows the established IL-17A class. Differentiation rests on regional availability, with no comparative data in the sources.
An oral TYK2 follower with no head-to-head data against SoC.

differentiation.comparator_evidence: Ph3 and Ph2 trials, placebo-controlled only.
differentiation.differentiation_vs_soc: An oral TYK2 follower with no comparative data against SoC.
A novel-mechanism oral agent outside the current SoC mechanism classes. Efficacy relative to SoC is unproven in these sources.

lessons.text: Recruitment failures cluster in Phase 3 and 2 trials with placebo or active-comparator designs in a crowded psoriasis field, including secukinumab and brodalumab, so enrollment feasibility and eligibility criteria need pre-testing.

Many terminations are sponsor business or portfolio decisions across modalities (mirikizumab, BI 730357, cedirogant, ZL-1102, XmAb27564) rather than documented efficacy failures, so they should not be counted as target invalidation.
Local tolerability can end development of an injectable biologic: injection site reactions met protocol-defined stopping criteria for teplizumab.
Regulatory interaction is a distinct risk: an FDA request halted the pefcalcitol ointment study before enrollment, so early agency alignment matters.
Several stops give no usable rationale, including withdrawn, suspended or deferred reasons, which limits cross-trial learning and argues for fuller registry disclosure.
Protocol redesign such as dose-regimen changes can end an early-phase trial without a scientific failure.

narrative.text: Innovation is industry-led: all of the top 15 sponsors by active Ph2/3 count are industry companies, with Janssen Research & Development the largest (5 active trials), followed by Oruka Therapeutics (4).

Chinese companies make up a large share of the leading sponsors, including Guangdong Hengrui, Haisco, Hansoh, InventisBio, InnoCare, CSPC Ouyi, Innovent, Jiangsu HengRui and Zhejiang Wenda, each with 2-3 active trials.

Trial activity is spread across the US, Poland, Hungary, Germany, Taiwan, Japan and China. Arlington Dermatology (US), Dermed Centrum Medyczne (Poland) and Peking University Third Hospital (China) lead with 7 trials each.

Key opinion leader signals are mostly publication-driven. Menter, Elmets, Sbidian, Le Cleach and Nast each have 2-3 key publications and no trials. Yuling Shi (Shanghai Dermatology Hospital) is the most active investigator with 2 trials as Principal Investigator.

claims.claim: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease and the most common psoriasis variant, with substantial physical, psychological and social impact.
claims.rationale: P32 states chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease with physical, psychological and social effects; P40 says plaque psoriasis is the most common variant.
claims.evidence_quote: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease that has considerable effects on patients' physical, psychological and social well-being.

claims.claim: Psoriasis is regarded as a systemic inflammatory disease with a major genetic component, associated with psoriatic arthritis and cardiometabolic, hepatic and psychological comorbidity.
claims.rationale: P34 gives the genetic component and the comorbidities; P30 describes systemic inflammatory disorder.
claims.evidence_quote: Its association with psoriatic arthritis and increased rates of cardiometabolic, hepatic and psychological comorbidity requires a holistic and multidisciplinary care approach.

claims.claim: Management is tailored to severity: topicals for mild disease; oral systemics and biologics (TNF, IL-17, IL-23, IL-12/23) for moderate-to-severe disease.
claims.rationale: Both sources describe topicals for mild disease and oral systemics plus biologics for moderate-to-severe disease.
claims.evidence_quote: Biologic therapies targeting TNF, IL-17, IL-23 and IL-12/23 have demonstrated high efficacy in improving both cutaneous and systemic inflammation.

claims.claim: Prevalence (estimated people affected) (Global): Approximately 125 million people worldwide. Review estimate; alternative estimate of 60 million people worldwide in another review.
claims.rationale: P40 gives 125 million and P34 gives 60 million worldwide.
claims.evidence_quote: Approximately 125 million people worldwide have psoriasis.

claims.claim: Prevalence (Global): Approximately 2% to 3% of the global population. Review-level estimates; one review states approximately 2% worldwide.
claims.rationale: P43 gives 2-3% and P42 gives approximately 2% worldwide.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting approximately 2 % to 3 % of the global population.

claims.claim: Prevalence (US adults): 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%); about 7.55 million US adults. NHANES 2011-2014, adults 20 years or older, self-reported physician diagnosis; translated using 2020 US census; no significant change since 2003.
claims.rationale: All details match P49; self-report of physician diagnosis is consistent with the survey question.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis prevalence among US adults 20 years or older was 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%). Based on the 2020 US census data, this outcome translates to an estimated 7.55 million US adults with psoriasis.

claims.claim: Prevalence (US): Up to 3.2% of the US population. Cited in AAD-NPF guidelines.
claims.rationale: All three guidelines state up to 3.2% of US population.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis is a chronic, inflammatory, multisystem disease that affects up to 3.2% of the United States population.

claims.claim: Prevalence (Western Europe): 1.92% (95% uncertainty interval 1.07%-3.46%). Bayesian hierarchical model from systematic review, data to October 2019. Central Europe 1.83% (0.62%-5.32%); North America 1.50% (0.63%-3.60%).
claims.rationale: Figures match P48.
claims.evidence_quote: The prevalence of psoriasis was also high in western Europe (1.92%, 1.07% to 3.46%), central Europe (1.83%, 0.62% to 5.32%), North America (1.50%, 0.63% to 3.60%)

claims.claim: Prevalence (Italy): 1.8%-3.1% in total population; 1.8%-4.8% in a second systematic review. Systematic reviews; regional prevalence varied 0.8-4.5%; mostly non-representative studies.
claims.rationale: Ranges match, but P53 gives 1.8%-4.8% (matching) while the claim's 'mostly non-representative' is supported; however the 0.8-4.5% regional range is in P51. Minor: the second review's range is accurate; overall fine except the claim blends them.
claims.evidence_quote: Prevalence of psoriasis in specific regions showed more variability (0.8-4.5%) than that in the total population (1.8-3.1%).

claims.claim: Prevalence (UK): 1.52% of the general population. Cited in brief overview.
claims.rationale: P34 states 1.52% in the UK.
claims.evidence_quote: with 1.52% of the general population affected in the UK

claims.claim: Incidence (Adults, country range (incl. Italy)): 30.3 per 100,000 person-years (Taiwan) to 321.0 per 100,000 person-years (Italy). Systematic review of general-population studies; 81% of countries lack epidemiology data.
claims.rationale: Incidence range and 81% figure match P48. Number(s) 81 not found in the cited source text.
claims.evidence_quote: the incidence of psoriasis varied from 30.3 per 100 000 person years (95% confidence interval 26.6 to 34.1) in Taiwan to 321.0 per 100 000 person years in Italy.

claims.claim: Prevalence in children (Europe): Up to 2% of children. Review of childhood psoriasis.
claims.rationale: P31 states up to 2% of children in Europe.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis affects up to 2% of children in Europe

claims.claim: Prevalence of psoriatic arthritis among psoriasis patients (Europe / North America / Global): 22.7% Europe; 19.5% North America; 19.7% pooled overall. Meta-analysis of 266 studies, 976,408 patients; pooled prevalence 3.3% in those under 18.
claims.rationale: All figures match P50.
claims.evidence_quote: the pooled proportion (95% confidence interval [CI]) of PsA among patients with psoriasis was 19.7% (95% CI, 18.5%-20.9%).

claims.claim: Topical-therapy candidates vs systemic-therapy candidates (dichotomous): Not reported in sources of patients (defined by International Psoriasis Council Delphi consensus: systemic candidates meet at least one of BSA >10%, involvement of special areas, or failure of topical therapy; replaces mild/moderate/severe categories.)
claims.rationale: P7 defines dichotomous categories with the stated criteria.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis patients should be classified as either candidates for topical therapy or candidates for systemic therapy; the latter are patients who meet at least one of the following criteria: (1) body surface area >10%, (2) disease involving special areas, and (3) failure of topical therapy.

claims.claim: Mild: Not reported in sources of patients (defined by Conventionally managed with topical therapy as first-line (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, calcineurin inhibitors).)
claims.rationale: Both sources state topicals are first-line for mild disease.
claims.evidence_quote: For mild disease, topical therapies remain the first-line treatment, including corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues and topical calcineurin inhibitors.

claims.claim: Moderate-to-severe: Not reported in sources of patients (defined by Conventionally requires systemic therapy (oral agents or biologics); biologics are an option for first-line treatment per AAD-NPF guidelines.)
claims.rationale: P40 notes AAD-NPF recommends biologics as first-line option for moderate to severe; oral systemics also described.
claims.evidence_quote: The American Academy of Dermatology-National Psoriasis Foundation guidelines recommend biologics as an option for first-line treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis

claims.claim: Basis: about 3.0% US adult prevalence (about 7.55 million adults); the share eligible for systemic therapy is not quantified in the sources.
claims.rationale: P49 gives 3.0% and 7.55 million; the sources do not quantify the systemic-eligible share.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis prevalence among US adults 20 years or older was 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%).

claims.claim: Systemic-therapy candidates are defined by BSA >10%, special-area involvement or topical failure, rather than by a fixed severity share.
claims.rationale: P7 defines systemic candidates by those criteria, not a fixed share.
claims.evidence_quote: the latter are patients who meet at least one of the following criteria: (1) body surface area >10%, (2) disease involving special areas, and (3) failure of topical therapy.

claims.claim: Adult-focused guidelines address moderate-to-severe disease; psoriasis occurs more often in adults than in children (up to 2% of European children).
claims.rationale: P5 addresses adults with moderate-to-severe; P48 says more frequent in adults; P31 up to 2% of European children.
claims.evidence_quote: The disease occurs more frequently in adults than in children.

claims.claim: Strong genetic predisposition: HLA-C*06:02 shows the strongest association, particularly in early-onset disease; loci include IL23A, IL12B and IL17RA, linking to IL-23/Th17 dysregulation.
claims.rationale: Matches P32.
claims.evidence_quote: with HLA-C*06:02 showing the strongest association, particularly in those with early-onset disease.

claims.claim: Dendritic cells, Th17 cells and keratinocytes form a pathogenic triad: dendritic cell TNF-α and IL-23 drive Th17 cells producing IL-17, IFN-γ and IL-22, causing keratinocyte activation and hyperproliferation.
claims.rationale: Matches P41.
claims.evidence_quote: Dendritic cells produce TNF-α and IL-23 to promote T cell differentiation toward TH17 cells that produce key psoriatic cytokines IL-17, IFN-γ, and IL-22.

claims.claim: Keratinocytes initiate and maintain inflammation, releasing antimicrobial peptides and danger signals that amplify the immune loop.
claims.rationale: P47 states keratinocytes' critical role in initiating and maintaining inflammation; P42 mentions antimicrobial peptides and danger signals from keratinocytes.
claims.evidence_quote: The critical role of keratinocytes in initiating and maintaining the inflammatory state

claims.claim: ILC3 cells producing IL-17 and IL-22 can induce psoriatic rash without T-cell/antigen interaction and are increased in blood and skin.
claims.rationale: P42 states these points.
claims.evidence_quote: ILC3 induces psoriasis rashes directly without T-cell/antigen interaction

claims.claim: Environmental triggers contribute, including stress, which 31-88% of patients report as a trigger, and microbiota changes.
claims.rationale: P29 gives the 31-88% stress figure; P46 links microbiota changes to pathogenesis; P35 notes environmental triggers.
claims.evidence_quote: In 31-88% of cases, patients report stress as being a trigger for their psoriasis.

claims.claim: Presents with rounded erythematous, dry, scaling plaques, with predilection for nails, scalp, genitalia, extensor surfaces and lumbosacral region.
claims.rationale: P36 contains only photo captions of plaques; it does not describe nail, scalp, genital, extensor or lumbosacral predilection.
claims.evidence_quote: Elbow and forearm with erythematous, well-demarcated, pink plaques with mild micaceous scale in a 42-year-old White woman.

claims.claim: Psoriasis is clinically heterogeneous: plaque, flexural, guttate, pustular or erythrodermic forms; plaque psoriasis is the most common.
claims.rationale: P34 lists the forms; P40 says plaque is most common variant.
claims.evidence_quote: Plaque psoriasis is the most common variant of psoriasis.

claims.claim: Generalized pustular psoriasis is a distinct, rare, potentially life-threatening entity with sterile pustules, differing from plaque psoriasis.
claims.rationale: P10 states GPP is rare, severe, potentially life-threatening, distinct from plaque psoriasis; sterile pustules in P8/P4.
claims.evidence_quote: GPP is a rare, severe, and potentially life-threatening condition that is distinct from plaque psoriasis.

claims.claim: Childhood disease resembles adult disease but with smaller plaques, finer scales and more facial and guttate involvement.
claims.rationale: P31 describes these features.
claims.evidence_quote: face involvement and guttate psoriasis are more common, plaques are often smaller, and scales are finer and softer than in adults

claims.claim: Psoriatic arthritis affects about 19.7% of psoriasis patients (pooled; 3.3% in under-18s).
claims.rationale: Pooled 19.7% and 3.3% in under-18s match.
claims.evidence_quote: the pooled proportion (95% CI) of PsA among patients with psoriasis was 19.7% (95% CI, 18.5%-20.9%). In children and adolescents (<18 years of age), the pooled prevalence was 3.3%

claims.claim: Cardiometabolic disease, including cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome, is associated with psoriasis, particularly severe disease.
claims.rationale: P42 links CVD and metabolic syndrome to psoriasis, particularly the severe type.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis is significantly associated with cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and inflammatory disorders, particularly the severe type.

claims.claim: Psychiatric disorders and depression are associated with psoriasis.
claims.rationale: P32 and P40 cite psychiatric disorders and depression.
claims.evidence_quote: Plaque psoriasis is associated with a number of comorbidities including psoriatic arthritis, cardiometabolic diseases, and depression.

claims.claim: Obesity is strongly associated with psoriasis and reduces biologic efficacy and drug survival.
claims.rationale: P12 states all elements.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis and obesity have a strong association. Obesity decreases efficacy of biologics and may decrease efficacy and potentiate side effects of conventional therapies. It also impacts drug survival.

claims.claim: Other associations include gastrointestinal disease, kidney disease, malignancy and infection.
claims.rationale: P30 lists these associations.
claims.evidence_quote: additional associations between psoriasis and cardiometabolic diseases, gastrointestinal diseases, kidney disease, malignancy, infection, and mood disorders

claims.claim: Psoriasis is a lifelong, chronic, relapsing-remitting disease.
claims.rationale: P34 says lifelong; P41 says chronic, relapsing-remitting.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis is one of the most common inflammatory skin diseases with a chronic, relapsing-remitting course.

claims.claim: Comorbidities contribute to increased morbidity and mortality; patients have higher cerebrovascular and cardiovascular disease and a younger age at death.
claims.rationale: P32 states increased morbidity and mortality; P33 states cerebral/cardiovascular disease and younger age at death.
claims.evidence_quote: Individuals with psoriasis were also found to have higher incidences of cerebral and cardiovascular diseases and a younger age at death compared to healthy individuals.

claims.claim: On-treatment remission is defined as BSA 0% or IGA 0 maintained for at least 6 months; PASI 75 is the minimum therapeutic target and PASI 90 or PASI <2 desirable.
claims.rationale: Both definitions are stated in P6 and P11.
claims.evidence_quote: A Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) 75 response is defined as the minimum therapeutic target, while PASI 90 or an absolute PASI <2 are considered desirable goals.

claims.claim: Efficacy / Durability: Remission benchmarks (BSA 0% or IGA 0 for 6 months) were only recently standardized; precision medicine to enhance treatment durability is an ongoing research goal.; clinical impact: Lack of benchmarks hinders aligned expectations and long-term coverage decisions.
claims.rationale: Remission definition and precision medicine goal are supported; 'only recently standardized' is loosely implied, and the clinical impact of lacking benchmarks is only partly stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Defining on-treatment remission in plaque psoriasis is important for benchmarking patient responses to therapies.

claims.claim: Efficacy in obesity: Obesity decreases efficacy of biologics and may decrease efficacy and potentiate side effects of conventional therapies; it also reduces drug survival.; clinical impact: Reduced response in a large comorbid subgroup.
claims.rationale: Matches P12; 'large subgroup' is framing.
claims.evidence_quote: Obesity decreases efficacy of biologics and may decrease efficacy and potentiate side effects of conventional therapies. It also impacts drug survival.

claims.claim: Safety & Tolerability: Special populations such as HIV-associated psoriasis show higher failure rates and need monitoring for opportunistic infections; paradoxical psoriasis occurs with some drugs.; clinical impact: Limited options and careful monitoring in complex patients.
claims.rationale: P38 gives higher failure rates and monitoring; P45 describes paradoxical psoriasis with drugs.
claims.evidence_quote: psoriasis tends to be more severe, to have atypical presentations and higher failure rates with the usual prescribed treatments

claims.claim: Comorbidity management: No clear guidelines on vascular testing in psoriasis, and treatment must be tailored around multiple comorbidities.; clinical impact: Increased cardiovascular and psychiatric burden persists.
claims.rationale: P33 says no clear guidelines on vascular testing; P39 on tailoring to comorbidities.
claims.evidence_quote: no clear guidelines have been defined regarding how much vascular lesion testing should be performed in patients with psoriasis

claims.claim: Severity classification / Undertreatment: Heterogeneous severity classifications ignore special areas and treatment history, so patients may be miscategorized.; clinical impact: Can lead to undertreatment.
claims.rationale: P7 states this.
claims.evidence_quote: owing to the heterogeneity of severity classifications and their lack of consideration for the impact of psoriasis involvement of special areas or past treatment history, patients may be miscategorized, which can lead to undertreatment

claims.claim: Pediatric evidence: Few data on epidemiology, comorbidity and therapy in children; international management guidelines are lacking.; clinical impact: Treatment choices rely on limited evidence.
claims.rationale: P31 states both.
claims.evidence_quote: Recently, few data have been published on epidemiology, comorbidity, or therapy in children with psoriasis.

claims.claim: The International Psoriasis Council Delphi consensus proposes a dichotomous classification in place of mild/moderate/severe: patients are candidates for topical therapy or for systemic therapy. Systemic candidates meet at least one criterion: BSA >10%, involvement of special areas, or failure of topical therapy.
claims.rationale: Matches P7.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis patients should be classified as either candidates for topical therapy or candidates for systemic therapy; the latter are patients who meet at least one of the following criteria: (1) body surface area >10%

claims.claim: Topical agents (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, calcineurin inhibitors, keratolytics) remain the mainstay for mild psoriasis. AAD-NPF guidelines recommend biologics as an option for first-line treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.
claims.rationale: Topical mainstay supported by P40; P3 abstract does not mention biologics, though P40 attributes AAD-NPF guideline recommendation.
claims.evidence_quote: The American Academy of Dermatology-National Psoriasis Foundation guidelines recommend biologics as an option for first-line treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis

claims.claim: The updated German S3 guideline (adapted from EuroGuiDerm) more prominently highlights first-line use of biologics or novel targeted small molecules and has added bimekizumab and deucravacitinib. It defines PASI 75 as the minimum therapeutic target, with PASI 90 or absolute PASI <2 as desirable goals.
claims.rationale: P11 states all.
claims.evidence_quote: the possibility of first-line therapy with biologics or novel targeted small molecules is more prominently highlighted

claims.claim: The 2025 French guidelines recommend methotrexate, adalimumab or ustekinumab as primary systemic treatment for patients without symptomatic comorbidities. The NPF consensus defines on-treatment remission as BSA 0% or IGA 0 maintained for at least 6 months on treatment.
claims.rationale: Both statements match P5 and P6.
claims.evidence_quote: The working group recommends methotrexate, adalimumab or ustekinumab as the primary systemic treatment for patients with psoriasis without symptomatic comorbidities.

claims.claim: First-line for Mild disease / candidates for topical therapy (BSA <=10%, no special-area involvement, no topical failure): Topical corticosteroids, Vitamin D analogues, Topical calcineurin inhibitors, Keratolytics. Topical therapy is the mainstay for mild psoriasis; the IPC dichotomy assigns patients not meeting systemic criteria to topical therapy.
claims.rationale: Topical agents and IPC dichotomy supported by P40 and P7.
claims.evidence_quote: For patients with mild psoriasis, topical agents remain the mainstay of treatment, and they include topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, calcineurin inhibitors, and keratolytics.

claims.claim: First-line for Moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in adults (systemic candidates: BSA >10%, special areas, or topical failure): Biologics (TNF-alpha, IL-12/23, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors), Novel targeted small molecules (apremilast, deucravacitinib). AAD-NPF guidelines recommend biologics as first-line options for moderate-to-severe disease. The German S3 guideline highlights first-line biologics or novel small molecules.
claims.rationale: Biologics first-line and German guideline supported; deucravacitinib/apremilast as first-line small molecules only partly stated (P11 names novel small molecules, deucravacitinib incorporated).
claims.evidence_quote: the possibility of first-line therapy with biologics or novel targeted small molecules is more prominently highlighted

claims.claim: First-line for Adults with moderate-to-severe psoriasis without symptomatic comorbidities (French guidelines 2025): Methotrexate, Adalimumab, Ustekinumab. The French working group recommends these as the primary systemic treatment.
claims.rationale: Matches P5.
claims.evidence_quote: The working group recommends methotrexate, adalimumab or ustekinumab as the primary systemic treatment for patients with psoriasis without symptomatic comorbidities.

claims.claim: Second-line for Inadequate response, low disease activity, or need to switch, long-term management of moderate-to-severe disease: Switch to another biologic or targeted agent, Conventional systemics (methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin, fumarates). EuroGuiDerm covers conventional and biologic systemics. French guidelines include recommendations for insufficient response. Biologics show a longer time to relapse than oral systemic agents after discontinuation.
claims.rationale: EuroGuiDerm drugs, French insufficient-response recommendations and longer relapse time for biologics are supported, but 'switch to another biologic' as second-line is not stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Biological agents are associated with a longer time to relapse than oral systemic agents after drug discontinuation.

claims.claim: Second-line for Guttate psoriasis not controlled with topicals/phototherapy: Methotrexate, Cyclosporine. A systematic review proposes methotrexate or cyclosporine as second-line for guttate psoriasis. First-line is topical corticosteroids and calcipotriol with phototherapy.
claims.rationale: P15 recommends methotrexate or cyclosporine as second-line and topical corticosteroids plus calcipotriol with phototherapy as first-line.
claims.evidence_quote: As first-line therapy, we recommend topical corticosteroids and calcipotriol cream, in combination with phototherapy.

claims.claim: Third-line / Refractory for Severe and refractory guttate psoriasis: Biologics. The proposed algorithm positions biologics as third-line for severe and refractory guttate psoriasis.
claims.rationale: P15 states biologics can be used as third-line for severe and refractory GP.
claims.evidence_quote: For severe and refractory GP, biologics can be used as third-line treatment.

claims.claim: Third-line / Refractory for Patients with obesity (reduced efficacy of biologics) and special populations such as ICI-induced psoriasis: Weight control with optimized systemic therapy, Non-steroid systemic agents for ICI-induced psoriasis. Obesity decreases biologic efficacy and weight control is vital. For ICI-induced psoriasis, systemic agents may be used without appreciable loss of ICI effectiveness, with non-steroid agents preferred over systemic corticosteroids.
claims.rationale: P12 says obesity decreases biologic efficacy and weight control is vital; P18 says systemic agents may be used without appreciable loss of ICI effectiveness and non-steroid agents are preferred.
claims.evidence_quote: saPs may be used to treat ICI-Ps without an appreciable loss of ICI effectiveness.

claims.claim: TNF-alpha (TNF inhibitor biologics, e.g. etanercept, adalimumab, certolizumab pegol, infliximab): Neutralize TNF-alpha, a cytokine produced by dendritic cells that promotes T cell differentiation toward TH17 cells.. Reduces upstream drivers of the IL-23/IL-17 axis, decreasing keratinocyte activation and skin inflammation.
claims.rationale: Sources support TNF-α from dendritic cells promoting TH17 and TNF inhibitors existing, but not explicitly that these inhibitors reduce upstream IL-23/IL-17 drivers; the mechanism is inferred.
claims.evidence_quote: Dendritic cells produce TNF-α and IL-23 to promote T cell differentiation toward TH17 cells that produce key psoriatic cytokines IL-17, IFN-γ, and IL-22.

claims.claim: IL-12/23 (p40) (IL-12/23 inhibitor biologic, e.g. ustekinumab): Binds the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23.. Dampens IL-23-driven TH17 differentiation and IL-17/IL-22 production.
claims.rationale: P40 states ustekinumab inhibits p40 of IL-12/23 (as IL-12 and 'IL-13' typo), and P41 describes IL-23 driving TH17; the dampening effect is an inference.
claims.evidence_quote: inhibit cytokines such as the p40 subunit of the cytokines IL-12 and IL-13 (ustekinumab)

claims.claim: IL-23 (p19) (IL-23 p19 inhibitor biologics, e.g. guselkumab, tildrakizumab, risankizumab, mirikizumab): Selectively inhibit the p19 subunit of IL-23, produced by dendritic cells.. Reduces TH17 and ILC3 maturation and IL-17/IL-22 output, resolving keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Longest time to relapse after discontinuation among biologics.
claims.rationale: Sources cover p19 inhibitors, DC IL-23, ILC3 maturation with IL-23 and IL-17/IL-22 production, and longest relapse time for IL-23 antagonists.
claims.evidence_quote: Among biologicals, IL-23 antagonists are associated with the longest time to relapse.

claims.claim: IL-17 (IL-17 pathway inhibitor biologics, e.g. secukinumab, ixekizumab, brodalumab, bimekizumab): Inhibit IL-17 cytokines (brodalumab acts at the IL-17 pathway).. Blocks the effector cytokine from TH17 cells and ILC3s on keratinocytes, reducing epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation.
claims.rationale: Sources list IL-17 inhibitors and IL-17 production by TH17/ILC3, but the P2/P11 abstracts do not state the mechanism or the brodalumab IL-17 pathway detail; effects on epidermal hyperplasia are inferred.
claims.evidence_quote: IL-17 (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab, and brodalumab)

claims.claim: PDE4 (Oral small molecule, e.g. apremilast): Inhibits phosphodiesterase 4.. Modulates intracellular inflammatory signalling (PDE-4 pathway) in psoriasis pathogenesis.
claims.rationale: P40 identifies apremilast as a PDE4 inhibitor and P43 names the PDE-4 pathway in pathogenesis.
claims.evidence_quote: the advanced small molecule apremilast, which is a phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor

claims.claim: TYK2 (Oral targeted small molecule, e.g. deucravacitinib): Tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor, acting in the JAK-STAT signalling pathway.. Dampens cytokine signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway implicated in psoriasis.
claims.rationale: Sources mention deucravacitinib and JAK-STAT pathway in psoriasis, and TYK2 small molecules, but do not explicitly say deucravacitinib is a TYK2 inhibitor acting in JAK-STAT.
claims.evidence_quote: Various signalling pathways, including NF-κB, JAK-STAT, S1P, PDE-4, and A3AR that are involved in the pathogenesis of psoriasis

claims.claim: Risankizumab (IL-23 p19 inhibitor; target IL-23 (p19)): PASI 90 71.6% (95% CrI 67.5%-75.4%) at weeks 10-16; 79.4% (95% CI 75.5%-82.9%) at weeks 44-60 (network meta-analysis, JAMA Dermatol 2020). Safety: Not reported in the provided sources.
claims.rationale: Numbers match P22.
claims.evidence_quote: risankizumab-rzaa (71.6%; 95% credible interval [CrI], 67.5%-75.4%)

claims.claim: Brodalumab (IL-17 pathway inhibitor; target IL-17): PASI 90 70.8% (95% CrI 66.8%-74.6%) at weeks 10-16; 74.0% (95% CI 69.3%-78.1%) at weeks 44-60 (network meta-analysis, JAMA Dermatol 2020). Safety: Not reported in the provided sources.
claims.rationale: Brodalumab numbers match P22.

claims.claim: Ixekizumab (IL-17A inhibitor; target IL-17): PASI 90 70.6% (95% CrI 66.8%-74.6%) at weeks 10-16; 73.9% (95% CI 69.9%-77.5%) at weeks 44-60 (network meta-analysis, JAMA Dermatol 2020). Safety: Not reported in the provided sources.
claims.rationale: Ixekizumab numbers match P22.

claims.claim: Guselkumab (IL-23 p19 inhibitor; target IL-23 (p19)): PASI 90 67.3% (95% CrI 62.5%-71.9%) at weeks 10-16; 76.5% (95% CI 72.1%-80.5%) at weeks 44-60 (network meta-analysis, JAMA Dermatol 2020). Safety: Not reported in the provided sources.
claims.rationale: Guselkumab numbers match P22.

claims.claim: The pipeline is dominated by oral TYK2 inhibitors (zasocitinib, envudeucitinib, ICP-488, SYHX1901, TQH3906, D-2570 and others), most in Ph3. This is crowded, and deucravacitinib is already SoC.
claims.rationale: Records show these as Ph3 oral agents, but the sources never identify them as TYK2 inhibitors (except D-2570 vs BMS-986165 comparator), nor that deucravacitinib is SoC or that the pipeline is dominated by them.
claims.evidence_quote: Drug: D-2570 Tablet, Drug: BMS-986165 Tablet

claims.claim: Head-to-head designs against SoC are the strongest evidence. They include icotrokinra versus deucravacitinib, picankibart versus secukinumab and ixekizumab, netakimab versus adalimumab, and deucravacitinib and bimekizumab versus ustekinumab.
claims.rationale: Head-to-head designs exist (icotrokinra vs deucravacitinib, picankibart vs IL-17 mAbs, netakimab vs adalimumab), but bimekizumab vs ustekinumab is not in the sources and 'strongest evidence' is an unsupported judgement.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] ADA: Drug: Adalimumab - adalimumab given subcutaneously during main period

claims.claim: The oral IL-23 receptor peptide icotrokinra aims to pair biologic-like IL-23 pathway blockade with oral convenience.
claims.rationale: Records show JNJ-77242113 trials but do not describe it as an oral IL-23 receptor peptide named icotrokinra.
claims.evidence_quote: A Study of JNJ-77242113 for the Treatment of Participants With Moderate to Severe Plaque Psoriasis (ICONIC-ADVANCE 2)

claims.claim: Several assets are biosimilars or follow-ons (CT-P55 versus Cosentyx, QL2106 versus Tremfya) that differentiate on cost and access rather than efficacy.
claims.rationale: Records show comparisons with Cosentyx and Tremfya, but nothing says they are biosimilars differentiating on cost and access.
claims.evidence_quote: A Study to Compare Efficacy and Safety of CT-P55 and Cosentyx in Patients With Moderate to Severe Psoriasis

claims.claim: Many early assets (e.g., CMS-D001, WD-890, HS-20118) are placebo-controlled with undisclosed mechanisms. Their differentiation versus SoC cannot yet be assessed.
claims.rationale: The three records are placebo-controlled with no mechanism disclosed.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Group 2: Placebo: Drug: Drug: placebo

claims.claim: JNJ-77242113 (icotrokinra) (Peptide; IL-23 receptor): Ph3 program with placebo-controlled and dose-comparison designs, plus a placebo- and active-controlled study against deucravacitinib (SoC). Head-to-head versus an oral SoC is stronger evidence than placebo alone.
claims.rationale: Placebo and deucravacitinib-controlled designs are shown, but the peptide/IL-23R antagonist description and SoC status are not in the sources, nor are explicit dose-comparison designs.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Deucravacitinib: Drug: JNJ-77242113, Drug: JNJ-77242113 Matching Placebo, Drug: Deucravacitinib

claims.claim: Zasocitinib (TAK-279) (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 trials are placebo-controlled or dose-comparison, plus one single-arm study. No head-to-head SoC comparator is listed in these trials, so the evidence is weaker.
claims.rationale: The cited zasocitinib trials (T62, T16, T30) are single-arm, placebo-controlled and open-label with no SoC comparator, but the sources show no dose-comparison arm and only T16 has a placebo arm; the 'plus one single-arm' count is inexact.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Part A (Cohort 1 and Cohort 2): Placebo: Drug: Placebo

claims.claim: Deucravacitinib (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 trials with placebo and an active ustekinumab (SoC) comparator. These are new studies of an already-approved SoC agent.
claims.rationale: T57 has an ustekinumab comparator and T13 has placebo, but the sources do not say these are new studies of an already-approved agent.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Arm B: Drug: Ustekinumab

claims.claim: Picankibart (IBI112) (Monoclonal antibody; IL-23 (p19)): One Ph3 trial is head-to-head against active IL-17 biologics (secukinumab, ixekizumab; SoC), which is strong evidence. A second Ph3 trial is placebo-controlled.
claims.rationale: T32 has secukinumab/ixekizumab active comparator arms and T53 is placebo-controlled.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] IL-17 mAb continued treatment group: Drug: Picankibart, Drug: Secukinumab, Drug: Placebo, Drug: Ixekizumab

claims.claim: Bimekizumab (Monoclonal antibody; IL-17A/IL-17F): Trial designs include an active ustekinumab (SoC) comparator, an active clobetasol comparator, no-treatment and single-arm designs. Evidence quality varies across studies.
claims.rationale: The sources show ustekinumab comparator (T19), clobetasol comparator (T25), a no-intervention healthy control cohort (T17) and a single-arm design (T1).
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Comparator group Clobetasol: Drug: Clobetasol

claims.claim: Netakimab (Monoclonal antibody; IL-17A): Ph3 trial with placebo and an active adalimumab (SoC) comparator, so head-to-head evidence against a TNF inhibitor is planned.
claims.rationale: T28 has placebo and adalimumab active comparator arms in a Phase 3 trial.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] ADA: Drug: Adalimumab - adalimumab given subcutaneously during main period

claims.claim: TQH3906 (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 trial with active deucravacitinib 6 mg (SoC) and placebo arms. This is a head-to-head against the approved TYK2 inhibitor.
claims.rationale: T35 has a deucravacitinib 6 mg active comparator and a placebo arm in a Phase 3 trial.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] TQH3906 Capsules placebo + Deucravacitinib tablets 6 mg

claims.claim: D-2570 (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 and Ph2 trials with placebo and an active BMS-986165 (deucravacitinib code name; SoC) arm.
claims.rationale: Only T6 has a BMS-986165 active arm; T38 and T10 are placebo-only, so the claim overgeneralizes.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Evaluate the efficacy of different doses of D-2570 compared with BMS-98165

claims.claim: CT-P55 (Biosimilar; IL-17A): Ph3 trial against EU-approved Cosentyx, a biosimilar equivalence design.
claims.rationale: T22 compares CT-P55 against EU-approved Cosentyx in Phase 3; the equivalence framing is reasonable analysis.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] EU-approved Cosentyx: Biological: CT-P55, Biological: EU-approved Cosentyx

claims.claim: QL2106 (Monoclonal antibody; IL-23 (p19)): Ph3 trial against active Tremfya (guselkumab), most likely an equivalence design.
claims.rationale: T52 is Phase 3 with a Tremfya active comparator; 'most likely equivalence' is hedged.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Tremfya®: Drug: Tremfya®

claims.claim: Envudeucitinib (Alumis) (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 trial with placebo only, with no active SoC comparator. Evidence is weaker than head-to-head.
claims.rationale: T50 has open-label, blinded and placebo arms only and no active comparator.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Drug: Placebo - Matching placebo administered as an oral tablet

claims.claim: SHR-1314 (vunakizumab) (Monoclonal antibody; IL-17A): Ph3 single-arm trial, which is the weakest design.
claims.rationale: T36 is Phase 3 with a single SHR-1314 arm.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [EXPERIMENTAL] SHR-1314: Drug: SHR-1314

claims.claim: ICP-488 (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 placebo-controlled only.
claims.rationale: T3 is Phase 3 with ICP-488 versus placebo only.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] ICP-488 Placebo: Drug: ICP-488 Placebo

claims.claim: SYHX1901 (Oral small molecule; TYK2): Ph3 and Ph2 trials, placebo-controlled only.
claims.rationale: T9 (Ph3) and T15 (Ph2) both have placebo comparators and no active comparator.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Drug: Placebo

claims.claim: Piclidenoson (Oral small molecule; A3 adenosine receptor): Ph3 placebo-controlled only.
claims.rationale: T24 is Phase 3 with piclidenoson versus placebo only.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [PLACEBO_COMPARATOR] Placebo: Drug: Placebo

claims.claim: MK-3222 200 mg (NCT01936688) was withdrawn; cause categorized as other / unspecified. Withdrawn Phase 3 with no stated reason in the registry, so no efficacy or safety inference can be drawn.
claims.rationale: T70 is withdrawn Phase 3 with no 'why stopped' given.
claims.evidence_quote: Status: withdrawn; Phase: Ph3; Sponsor: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited (industry)

claims.claim: DFD01 Spray (NCT02527421) was terminated; cause categorized as enrollment / feasibility. Enrollment criteria were too restrictive to recruit patients, so eligibility criteria should be feasibility-tested before launching a Phase 3.
claims.rationale: The record states the trial was terminated for inability to recruit under current enrollment criteria; the recommendation is analytic.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Not able to recruit patients with the current enrollment criteria.

claims.claim: Investigational Arm - secukinumab (NCT04237116) was terminated; cause categorized as enrollment / feasibility. Low enrollment ended a placebo-controlled secukinumab Phase 3, showing recruitment risk in a crowded psoriasis field with many approved biologics.
claims.rationale: Terminated for low enrollment, placebo-controlled secukinumab Phase 3; the crowded-field comment is interpretive.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Low enrollment

claims.claim: Mirikizumab (NCT03556202) was terminated; cause categorized as business / strategic. Termination was a sponsor strategic decision, not evidence of efficacy or safety failure of mirikizumab.
claims.rationale: Termination was due to a sponsor strategic business decision.
claims.evidence_quote: The study was terminated due to a strategic business decision made by the Sponsor.

claims.claim: Brodalumab (NCT04305327) was terminated; cause categorized as enrollment / feasibility. Difficulty recruiting ended the brodalumab trial early, suggesting a placebo plus active-comparator design is hard to enroll for an established class.
claims.rationale: Terminated for difficulty recruiting; the trial had placebo and ustekinumab active comparator arms.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Early terminated due to difficulty recruiting participants

claims.claim: PH-10 (rose bengal disodium 0.001%), Control (NCT00555646) was terminated; cause categorized as other / unspecified. Stopped to change the dose regimen under a new protocol, which is a design revision rather than a documented efficacy or safety failure.
claims.rationale: Stopped for change of dose regimen (new protocol); no efficacy or safety failure is stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Change of dose regimen (new protocol)

claims.claim: teplizumab (NCT00954915) was terminated; cause categorized as safety. Injection site reactions met protocol-defined stopping criteria, so local tolerability can limit development of a parenteral antibody.
claims.rationale: Stopped because injection site reaction met protocol-defined stopping criteria.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Injection site reaction met protocol-defined stopping criteria.

claims.claim: mometasone furoate + salicylic acid (NCT01228656) was suspended; cause categorized as other / unspecified. The trial was suspended with no reason given, so no failure mechanism can be inferred.
claims.rationale: T78 is suspended with no reason given.
claims.evidence_quote: Status: suspended; Phase: Ph2; Sponsor: Azidus Brasil (industry)

claims.claim: DFD06 (NCT03179605) was terminated; cause categorized as enrollment / feasibility. Enrollment difficulty stopped a single-arm Phase 2, so recruitment feasibility should be confirmed before launch.
claims.rationale: Terminated for difficulty in enrollment; single-arm open-label Phase 2.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Difficulty in enrollment

claims.claim: pefcalcitol ointment, 0.005% (NCT02970331) was withdrawn; cause categorized as regulatory. The FDA requested the study be stopped, so regulatory alignment must be secured before starting a trial.
claims.rationale: Withdrawn because the FDA requested the study be stopped.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: FDA requested us to stop the study

claims.claim: BI 730357 (NCT03835481) was terminated; cause categorized as business / strategic. Company decision with no stated scientific reason, so it should not be treated as an efficacy failure of BI 730357.
claims.rationale: Terminated due to company decision with no scientific reason stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Due to company decision.

claims.claim: Cedirogant (NCT05044234) was terminated; cause categorized as business / strategic. Company decision with no efficacy or safety detail given for cedirogant, so the reason for stopping is not scientifically attributable.
claims.rationale: Record shows terminated with 'Company Decision' and no efficacy/safety reason given.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Company Decision

claims.claim: ZL-1102 1% w/w gel BID for 16 weeks, ZL-1102 3% w/w gel BID for 16 weeks (NCT06380907) was terminated; cause categorized as business / strategic. Sponsor decision without stated scientific rationale, so no efficacy or safety conclusion about ZL-1102 can be drawn.
claims.rationale: Terminated with 'Sponsor decision' and no scientific rationale; the claim omits the 3% QD arm, which is minor.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Sponsor decision

claims.claim: IRX4204 (NCT06723171) was suspended; cause categorized as other / unspecified. Sponsor-requested hold without a stated reason, so the cause of the pause is unclear.
claims.rationale: Suspended due to sponsor request for hold, no reason stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Sponsor request for study hold

claims.claim: ILV-095 300 mg in a 4 to 1 ratio (NCT01010542) was terminated; cause categorized as other / unspecified. The stop reason is deferred to a detailed description and not stated in the registry field, so the cause cannot be classified.
claims.rationale: Stop reason deferred to detailed description, not given in the field.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: See termination reason in detailed description.

claims.claim: XmAb27564 (NCT06005792) was terminated; cause categorized as business / strategic. A business decision ended the Phase 1 trial of XmAb27564, which is not evidence of a scientific failure.
claims.rationale: Phase 1 trial terminated for business decision.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Business Decision

claims.claim: Recruitment failures cluster in Phase 3 and 2 trials with placebo or active-comparator designs in a crowded psoriasis field, including secukinumab and brodalumab, so enrollment feasibility and eligibility criteria need pre-testing.
claims.rationale: Low enrollment/recruitment difficulty is stated for these trials, but the 'crowded field' and 'cluster' framing is not in the sources, and T76 is Ph3 with no placebo arm, T67 is single-arm.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Early terminated due to difficulty recruiting participants

claims.claim: Many terminations are sponsor business or portfolio decisions across modalities (mirikizumab, BI 730357, cedirogant, ZL-1102, XmAb27564) rather than documented efficacy failures, so they should not be counted as target invalidation.
claims.rationale: All five cited trials were stopped for business/company/strategic decisions with no efficacy failure documented.
claims.evidence_quote: The study was terminated due to a strategic business decision made by the Sponsor.

claims.claim: Local tolerability can end development of an injectable biologic: injection site reactions met protocol-defined stopping criteria for teplizumab.
claims.rationale: Teplizumab trial stopped because injection site reaction met stopping criteria.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Injection site reaction met protocol-defined stopping criteria.

claims.claim: Regulatory interaction is a distinct risk: an FDA request halted the pefcalcitol ointment study before enrollment, so early agency alignment matters.
claims.rationale: FDA request to stop is stated and study is withdrawn (enrollment n/a), but 'early agency alignment matters' is inference.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: FDA requested us to stop the study

claims.claim: Several stops give no usable rationale, including withdrawn, suspended or deferred reasons, which limits cross-trial learning and argues for fuller registry disclosure.
claims.rationale: T71 and T68 give no usable reason and T78 (suspended) lists none, but T70 (withdrawn) has no stop reason field at all; the call for disclosure is inference.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Sponsor request for study hold

claims.claim: Protocol redesign such as dose-regimen changes can end an early-phase trial without a scientific failure.
claims.rationale: Trial terminated for change of dose regimen with new protocol, not a stated scientific failure.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Change of dose regimen (new protocol)

claims.claim: Innovation is industry-led: all of the top 15 sponsors by active Ph2/3 count are industry companies, with Janssen Research & Development the largest (5 active trials), followed by Oruka Therapeutics (4).
claims.rationale: DERIVED ranking shows Janssen 5 and Oruka 4 leading; the top 15 listed are all companies, and sponsors are mostly industry. Number(s) 15 not found in the cited source text.
claims.evidence_quote: Janssen Research & Development, LLC 5, 5; Oruka Therapeutics, Inc. 4, 4;

claims.claim: Chinese companies make up a large share of the leading sponsors, including Guangdong Hengrui, Haisco, Hansoh, InventisBio, InnoCare, CSPC Ouyi, Innovent, Jiangsu HengRui and Zhejiang Wenda, each with 2-3 active trials.
claims.rationale: DERIVED sponsor ranking lists all the named Chinese sponsors with 2-3 active trials each (Guangdong Hengrui 3, Haisco 3, Hansoh 3, InventisBio 3, InnoCare 2, CSPC Ouyi 2, Innovent 2, Jiangsu HengRui 2, Zhejiang Wenda 2).
claims.evidence_quote: Guangdong Hengrui Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd 3, 3; Haisco Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd. 3, 3; Hansoh BioMedical R&D Company 3, 3; InventisBio Co., Ltd 3, 3

claims.claim: Trial activity is spread across the US, Poland, Hungary, Germany, Taiwan, Japan and China. Arlington Dermatology (US), Dermed Centrum Medyczne (Poland) and Peking University Third Hospital (China) lead with 7 trials each.
claims.rationale: DERIVED trial-center tallies include centers in all the listed countries; Arlington Dermatology, Dermed and Peking University Third Hospital each have 7 trials (Dermed is also at 7).
claims.evidence_quote: Arlington Dermatology (United States) 7; Dermed Centrum Medyczne Sp z o o (Poland) 7; Peking University Third Hospital (China) 7

claims.claim: Key opinion leader signals are mostly publication-driven. Menter, Elmets, Sbidian, Le Cleach and Nast each have 2-3 key publications and no trials. Yuling Shi (Shanghai Dermatology Hospital) is the most active investigator with 2 trials as Principal Investigator.
claims.rationale: Publication counts are right for Menter, Elmets, Sbidian and Le Cleach (3 each) and Nast (2), all with 0 trials. Yuling Shi has 2 trials as PI, but being the 'most active' investigator is not clearly supported, since others also have trials and a tie is possible.
claims.evidence_quote: Yuling Shi - 2 trials, 0 publications, Principal Investigator, Shanghai Dermatology Hospital

claims.claim: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated systemic inflammatory disease. US adult prevalence is 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%), about 7.55 million adults (NHANES 2011-2014), and Western Europe prevalence is 1.92%.
claims.rationale: P32/P34 support chronic immune-mediated disease with systemic inflammation, P49 supports the US figures, and P48 gives Western Europe 1.92%.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis prevalence among US adults 20 years or older was 3.0% (95% CI, 2.6%-3.4%). Based on the 2020 US census data, this outcome translates to an estimated 7.55 million US adults with psoriasis.

claims.claim: Biologics have set a high efficacy bar. In a 2020 network meta-analysis, PASI 90 at weeks 10-16 was 71.6% for risankizumab, 70.8% for brodalumab, 70.6% for ixekizumab and 67.3% for guselkumab.
claims.rationale: The PASI 90 values at weeks 10-16 match P22 for all four agents (the source gives 70.6% for ixekizumab).

claims.claim: Guidelines are shifting toward earlier advanced therapy. AAD-NPF supports biologics as a first-line option, and the German S3 guideline highlights first-line biologics or novel small molecules, adds bimekizumab and deucravacitinib, and sets PASI 90 or absolute PASI <2 as desirable goals.
claims.rationale: P11 supports the German S3 details. The AAD-NPF guideline P3 covers only topical and alternative therapy and does not mention biologics as first-line.
claims.evidence_quote: in this updated version, the possibility of first-line therapy with biologics or novel targeted small molecules is more prominently highlighted

claims.claim: The pipeline of 63 active trials is dominated by oral TYK2 inhibitors, most in Ph3, while deucravacitinib is already standard of care. This creates a crowded follower class.
claims.rationale: The cited trials include non-TYK2 agents (e.g. JNJ-77242113). The DERIVED counts do not show TYK2 dominance, and nothing in them states deucravacitinib is standard of care or that the class is crowded.
claims.evidence_quote: By phase: Ph3 29, Ph2 25, Ph1 5, Ph2/Ph3 2, Ph1/Ph2 2

claims.claim: Head-to-head trials against standard-of-care agents are the key differentiation evidence. Examples include icotrokinra vs deucravacitinib, picankibart vs secukinumab/ixekizumab, netakimab vs adalimumab, and bimekizumab and deucravacitinib vs ustekinumab.
claims.rationale: Icotrokinra (JNJ-77242113) vs deucravacitinib, picankibart vs IL-17 mAbs and netakimab vs adalimumab are supported. T13 has no ustekinumab comparator, T17 is a biomarker study with no ustekinumab arm, and the claim of 'key differentiation evidence' is not stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Adalimumab: Drug: Adalimumab - adalimumab given subcutaneously during main period

claims.claim: Most discontinuations reflect enrollment difficulty or business decisions rather than target invalidation. Low enrollment ended placebo-controlled secukinumab and brodalumab Ph3 trials in the crowded field.
claims.rationale: Low enrollment stopped the secukinumab trial and difficulty recruiting stopped the brodalumab trial, but the other terminations were company or business decisions. Brodalumab's reason was difficulty recruiting, not strictly 'low enrollment', and 'most' is only loosely backed.
claims.evidence_quote: Why stopped: Low enrollment

claims.claim: Durable remission is unmet. On-treatment remission (BSA 0% or IGA 0 for at least 6 months) was only recently standardized, and precision medicine for durability remains a research goal.
claims.rationale: The remission definition is supported, and P32 supports precision medicine for durability. 'Only recently standardized' and 'unmet' are inferences not stated in the sources.
claims.evidence_quote: on-treatment remission in plaque psoriasis was defined as patients maintaining a BSA of 0% or IGA of 0 for at least 6 months while on treatment

claims.claim: Obesity reduces biologic efficacy and drug survival, leaving room for therapies with weight-independent efficacy.
claims.rationale: P12 supports reduced biologic efficacy and an impact on drug survival. The 'room for therapies with weight-independent efficacy' is an inference not in the source.
claims.evidence_quote: Obesity decreases efficacy of biologics and may decrease efficacy and potentiate side effects of conventional therapies. It also impacts drug survival.

claims.claim: Pediatric psoriasis has few data on epidemiology, comorbidity and therapy, and lacks international management guidelines. This supports dedicated pediatric programs.
claims.rationale: P31 says few data have been published on epidemiology, comorbidity and therapy in children, and that the challenge will be to propose international guidelines to manage them; the inference of dedicated programs is acceptable analytic framing.
claims.evidence_quote: Recently, few data have been published on epidemiology, comorbidity, or therapy in children with psoriasis.

claims.claim: Special populations such as HIV-associated psoriasis show higher failure rates and need monitoring for opportunistic infections. Patients with multiple comorbidities need safer targeted agents and care models that address systemic inflammation.
claims.rationale: P38 supports higher failure rates and monitoring for opportunistic infections in HIV-associated psoriasis, and P39 and P33 support comorbidities and systemic inflammation. The need for 'safer targeted agents' is not stated.
claims.evidence_quote: In this population, psoriasis tends to be more severe, to have atypical presentations and higher failure rates with the usual prescribed treatments.

claims.claim: Heterogeneous severity classifications can miscategorize patients and lead to undertreatment. The IPC dichotomous topical-vs-systemic framework opens earlier systemic use for patients with BSA >10%, special-area involvement or topical failure.
claims.rationale: P7 states that heterogeneous classifications may lead to miscategorization and undertreatment, and defines the dichotomous framework with BSA >10%, special areas and topical failure as systemic-therapy criteria.
claims.evidence_quote: Psoriasis patients should be classified as either candidates for topical therapy or candidates for systemic therapy; the latter are patients who meet at least one of the following criteria: (1) body surface area >10%

claims.claim: Janssen's oral IL-23 receptor peptide icotrokinra seeks biologic-like IL-23 blockade in a pill and is being tested head-to-head against deucravacitinib. Janssen is the most active sponsor, with 5 active Ph2/3 trials.
claims.rationale: Records show JNJ-77242113 tested against deucravacitinib and Janssen with 5 active trials, but the sources never name icotrokinra or describe it as an oral IL-23 receptor peptide.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] Deucravacitinib: Drug: JNJ-77242113, Drug: JNJ-77242113 Matching Placebo, Drug: Deucravacitinib

claims.claim: Multiple TYK2 followers are running Ph3 trials directly against deucravacitinib, including TQH3906 and D-2570, alongside Takeda's zasocitinib and Alumis' envudeucitinib.
claims.rationale: TQH3906 has a Ph3 trial against deucravacitinib and D-2570 against BMS-986165 (deucravacitinib), but the zasocitinib palmoplantar trial is single-arm and the envudeucitinib trial is placebo/open-label; neither is against deucravacitinib, and TYK2 mechanism is not stated.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] TQH3906 Capsules placebo + Deucravacitinib tablets 6 mg

claims.claim: Biosimilars and follow-ons will pressure pricing in the IL-17A and IL-23 classes: CT-P55 is being tested against Cosentyx and QL2106 against Tremfya.
claims.rationale: CT-P55 vs Cosentyx and QL2106 vs Tremfya comparisons are shown, but the pricing pressure and the biosimilar/follow-on framing are not stated in the sources.
claims.evidence_quote: Arm [ACTIVE_COMPARATOR] EU-approved Cosentyx: Biological: CT-P55, Biological: EU-approved Cosentyx

claims.claim: Chinese companies make up a large share of leading sponsors (Hengrui, Haisco, Hansoh, InventisBio, InnoCare, CSPC Ouyi, Innovent and others), many with undisclosed-mechanism assets.
claims.rationale: The listed Chinese sponsors appear in the sponsor ranking and records, but the claim that many have undisclosed-mechanism assets is only loosely inferable and Chinese companies are not quantified as a large share.
claims.evidence_quote: Guangdong Hengrui Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd 3, 3; Haisco Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd. 3, 3; Hansoh BioMedical R&D Company 3, 3; InventisBio Co., Ltd 3, 3

claims.claim: Picankibart is challenging IL-17A inhibitors head-to-head against secukinumab and ixekizumab. Bimekizumab's dual IL-17A/F blockade is being tested against ustekinumab.
claims.rationale: The picankibart switch trial involves secukinumab and ixekizumab, but it is a switching study in IL-17 inadequate responders. The bimekizumab record (BE UNIQUE) is a gene expression biomarker study with no ustekinumab comparator.
claims.evidence_quote: Drug: Picankibart, Drug: Secukinumab, Drug: Placebo, Drug: Ixekizumab
